ai.title: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Plasma exchange (PLEX) removes pathogenic plasma components and replaces them with donor plasma or albumin. It is life‑saving in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, thrombotic microangiopathy, and severe Guillain‑Barré syndrome, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: Plasma exchange is an extracorporeal procedure that separates plasma from cellular components, discards the plasma, and returns cells with replacement fluid. Diagnosis is clinical: a disease known to be mediated by circulating antibodies, immune complexes, or toxins and meeting urgency criteria.
b: Urgent indication: rapidly progressive renal failure (eGFR <30 ml/min) with a treatable antibody‑mediated disease
TTP suspicion: thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolysis, neurologic change, renal dysfunction, fever

sections.p: Severity is judged by organ dysfunction and rate of decline. In renal disease, a rise in serum creatinine >30 % within 48 h or eGFR <30 ml/min signals severe disease. In TTP, a PLASMIC score ≥6 predicts high risk and mandates immediate PLEX.
b: Renal: eGFR <30 ml/min or creatinine rise >30 %/48 h
TTP: PLASMIC score 6–7

sections.p: Conditions requiring PLEX fall into three groups: antibody‑mediated renal disease, thrombotic microangiopathy, and severe immune neuropathy.
b: Anti‑GBM disease (Goodpasture’s) – classic emergency in East Africa
ANCA‑associated vasculitis (pauci‑immune RPGN)
Lupus nephritis class III/IV with crescents
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
Atypical hemolytic‑uremic syndrome (aHUS) – consider if ADAMTS13 normal
Severe Guillain‑Barré syndrome (moderate‑severe, rapid progression)
Hyperviscosity from Waldenström macroglobulinemia (rare but possible)

sections.p: Patients present with organ‑specific signs reflecting the underlying disease. Renal presentations include hematuria, proteinuria, edema, and rapidly falling urine output. TTP shows the classic pentad, though often incomplete. GBS presents with ascending weakness, areflexia, and possible respiratory compromise.
b: Renal: new‑onset hypertension, oliguria, dark urine
TTP: thrombocytopenia <30 ×10⁹/L, schistocytes on smear
GBS: Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score ≤40

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm the pathogenic mechanism and guide urgency.

t.b: Is renal function rapidly deteriorating? A rise >30 % in 48 h or eGFR <30 ml/min triggers urgent PLEX.
Identify antibody‑mediated RPGN; positive results justify PLEX alongside immunosuppression.
Severely reduced (<10 %) confirms TTP; if unavailable, use PLASMIC score to decide on empiric PLEX.
Detect schistocytes indicating microangiopathic hemolysis; supports TTP/HUS diagnosis.
Distinguish demyelinating GBS from other neuropathies; if unavailable, rely on clinical severity.
Assess thrombocytopenia and rule out DIC; normal PT/aPTT favors TTP over DIC.

sections.p: Failure to start PLEX promptly can lead to irreversible organ loss or death. Procedure‑related complications must be anticipated.
b: Renal: progression to end‑stage renal disease within days
TTP: sudden neurologic decline, cardiac ischemia, or death
PLEX: hypotension, allergic reaction to replacement fluid, citrate‑induced hypocalcemia, line infection

sections.p: Treat the underlying disease while providing supportive care. PLEX replaces 1–1.5 plasma volumes per session, usually daily for 5–7 days, then taper based on response.
b: Renal antibody disease: high‑dose IV methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide or rituximab, plus daily PLEX until serology clears
TTP: immediate daily PLEX + caplacizumab (if available) + steroids; avoid plasma‑rich products that may contain anti‑ADAMTS13 antibodies
GBS: PLEX (5 exchanges) or IVIG; choose PLEX when IVIG unavailable or contraindicated (e.g., severe renal failure)
Replace plasma with fresh frozen plasma in antibody‑mediated disease; use albumin for TTP when plasma supply limited

sections.p: Monitor disease activity, renal function, platelet count, and neurologic status. Long‑term immunosuppression prevents relapse in vasculitis and anti‑GBM disease.
b: Renal: weekly creatinine, urine protein, repeat ANCA/anti‑GBM after 2 weeks
TTP: platelet count daily until >150 ×10⁹/L, then weekly for 1 month
GBS: serial MRC scores, respiratory function tests

sections.p: Conditions that mimic the indications for PLEX but require different therapy.
b: HUS (Shiga‑toxin) – supportive care, no PLEX unless ADAMTS13 low
Septic shock – vasopressors, antibiotics, not PLEX
Acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis – steroids, not PLEX

sections.p: Laboratory values may be falsely reassuring in resource‑limited settings.
b: Normal ADAMTS13 when assay unavailable – rely on PLASMIC score
Mildly elevated creatinine in malnourished patients – assess urine output and trend

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly falling urine output with rising creatinine
Progressive respiratory weakness (MRC sum score ≤40) in GBS

faq.q: Why is plasma exchange preferred over IVIG in severe GBS with renal failure?
faq.a: IVIG is cleared renally and can worsen fluid overload; PLEX removes pathogenic antibodies without adding volume.

faq.q: Can plasma exchange be done without apheresis machines?
faq.a: In low‑resource settings, manual plasma separation using centrifugation and bedside exchange is possible, though slower and less precise.

faq.q: What is the minimum number of exchanges needed for TTP?
faq.a: At least five daily exchanges until platelets normalize and hemolysis stops; continue until clinical remission.

exam: A 22‑year‑old with hematuria, rising creatinine (from 1.2 to 2.8 mg/dL in 48 h) and positive anti‑GBM antibodies – what is the next immediate step? — Start urgent plasma exchange together with high‑dose steroids; delay increases risk of irreversible renal loss.

A patient presents with thrombocytopenia (20 ×10⁹/L), schistocytes, and a PLASMIC score of 6 – what therapy should you initiate and why? — Begin daily plasma exchange immediately; the high PLASMIC score predicts TTP where PLEX is life‑saving.

In a child with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, ANCA negative but anti‑GBM positive, what adjunctive treatment accompanies plasma exchange? — High‑dose intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral taper; immunosuppression prevents further antibody production.

Why is fresh frozen plasma preferred over albumin as replacement fluid in anti‑GBM disease? — FFP supplies functional clotting factors and may contain anti‑GBM antibodies that competitively bind, aiding removal; albumin lacks these components.

A patient with severe GBS cannot receive IVIG due to renal impairment – how does plasma exchange improve outcomes? — It removes circulating auto‑antibodies and complement, halting nerve damage while avoiding nephrotoxic fluid load.

What are the main complications of plasma exchange you must monitor during the first session? — Hypotension, citrate‑induced hypocalcemia, allergic reaction to donor plasma, and line‑related infection; treat with fluids, calcium gluconate, antihistamines, and aseptic technique.
How would you manage a suspected TTP patient if ADAMTS13 testing is unavailable? — Use the PLASMIC score; if ≥6, start plasma exchange empirically while arranging transfer for definitive testing.

What distinguishes thrombotic microangiopathy requiring plasma exchange from typical sepsis‑associated coagulopathy? — TMA shows severe thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolysis, normal PT/aPTT, and often neurologic signs; sepsis usually has prolonged coagulation times and DIC features.
